verses.text: It is reported commonly that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not so much as named among the Gentiles, that one should have his father’s wife.
And ye are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, that he that hath done this deed might be taken away from among you.
For I verily, as absent in body, but present in spirit, have judged already, as though I were present, concerning him that hath so done this deed,
In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when ye are gathered together, and my spirit, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ,
To deliver such an one unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.
Your glorying is not good. Know ye not that a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump?
Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump, as ye are unleavened. For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us:
Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness; but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.
I wrote unto you in an epistle not to company with fornicators:
Yet not altogether with the fornicators of this world, or with the covetous, or extortioners, or with idolaters; for then must ye needs go out of the world.

But now I have written unto you not to keep company, if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat.
For what have I to do to judge them also that are without? do not ye judge them that are within?
But them that are without God judgeth. Therefore put away from among yourselves that wicked person.

summary: Paul turns from the parties and personalities of the first four chapters to a scandal that had become public knowledge: "It is reported commonly that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not so much as named among the Gentiles, that one should have his father’s wife." The offense is measured against pagan Corinth itself and found to exceed it. What appalls Paul as much as the deed is the congregation's posture toward it — "And ye are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, that he that hath done this deed might be taken away from among you." A community that should be in grief is instead inflated, and their self-satisfaction is treated as the deeper disease. Paul then renders a verdict at a distance: "For I verily, as absent in body, but present in spirit, have judged already, as though I were present, concerning him that hath so done this deed," and directs an action to be carried out "In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when ye are gathered together, and my spirit, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, To deliver such an one unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus." The sentence is severe and its stated aim is rescue. He then reaches for a proverb and a feast: "Your glorying is not good. Know ye not that a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump? Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump, as ye are unleavened. For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us: Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness; but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth." A previous letter had evidently been misread, and Paul corrects it: "I wrote unto you in an epistle not to company with fornicators: Yet not altogether with the fornicators of this world, or with the covetous, or extortioners, or with idolaters; for then must ye needs go out of the world." The line he is drawing runs inside the community, not around it: "But now I have written unto you not to keep company, if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat." The principle of jurisdiction follows — "For what have I to do to judge them also that are without? do not ye judge them that are within? But them that are without God judgeth" — and the chapter closes by putting an old command from Israel's law into the mouth of the church: "Therefore put away from among yourselves that wicked person."
takeaways: The chapter's sharpest rebuke is aimed at the congregation rather than at the offender. Paul states the sin in a single sentence and then spends the rest of the chapter on the church's reaction to it: "And ye are puffed up, and have not rather mourned." Tolerance here is not presented as generosity but as a species of pride, a community so pleased with its own broad-mindedness that it cannot feel the injury done in its midst. The prescribed emotion is grief — the man "might be taken away from among you" is stated as the thing they should have been mourning toward, not a punishment they should have been eager to inflict. Discipline that does not begin in mourning has already gone wrong.

The severity of the sentence is bounded by its purpose. "To deliver such an one unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh" is as harsh a phrase as Paul writes anywhere, and it is immediately given a redemptive end: "that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus." Exclusion is aimed at the man's salvation, not at the community's comfort or its reputation. This makes the measure medicinal rather than merely punitive, and it supplies the test by which any later act of the same kind must be judged: a discipline that has stopped hoping for the offender's restoration is no longer doing what Paul is doing here.

"Know ye not that a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump?" refuses the notion that serious sin can be a private matter within a body. The image is not of contagion by proximity but of a small quantity working invisibly through everything it touches, so that the question is never whether one man's conduct affects the whole but only how long the working takes. The corporate framing runs through the whole chapter — the church is a "lump," a "feast," a body that eats together — and it is why the remedy is corporate too, carried out "when ye are gathered together."

The Passover imagery grounds the command in something already accomplished rather than in something to be achieved. "Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump, as ye are unleavened" holds an imperative and an indicative in the same breath: become what you already are. The reason given is not the community's effort but a completed sacrifice — "For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us" — and the resulting life is described as an ongoing festival: "Therefore let us keep the feast... with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth." Holiness is presented as feasting rather than as fasting, the natural conduct of people for whom the deliverance has already happened.

Paul's correction of his earlier letter dismantles the instinct to withdraw from the world. He had written "not to company with fornicators," and someone had taken this as a program of separation from ordinary society; his answer is almost impatient — "for then must ye needs go out of the world." The boundary he is drawing runs through the church, not around it, applying to "any man that is called a brother." The claim to the name is precisely what makes the conduct a matter for the community, and its absence is precisely what puts the outsider beyond its reach.

The list of disqualifying sins quietly widens the scope past the scandal that prompted it. Alongside the fornicator stand "the covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner" — greed, abusive speech, and drunkenness placed in the same sentence as a sexual sin so notorious that pagans would not name it. A church willing to act on the spectacular offense and untroubled by the covetous man or the railer in good standing has not learned this chapter. Paul's final principle guards the other flank as well: "what have I to do to judge them also that are without? do not ye judge them that are within? But them that are without God judgeth." The community's competence is over its own members, and outsiders are left to a judgment that is not the church's to pronounce.

crossRefs.label: Leviticus 18:8 — The nakedness of thy father's wife shalt thou not uncover
crossRefs.why: The specific offense Paul names, "that one should have his father’s wife," is prohibited by name in the holiness legislation, where such unions are listed among the practices for which the land itself is said to vomit out its inhabitants. Reading the two together shows Paul is not improvising a rule for Corinth but applying a boundary the covenant community had always recognized, which is what makes the Corinthians' indifference so striking.

crossRefs.label: Deuteronomy 17:7 — So thou shalt put the evil away from among you
crossRefs.why: The chapter's closing command, "Therefore put away from among yourselves that wicked person," is drawn almost verbatim from the recurring refrain of Israel's judicial law. Paul transfers a formula originally attached to capital sentences in the covenant nation to the act of exclusion from the church, which both dignifies the seriousness of the measure and marks the change in its instrument, since the assembly removes a person from its fellowship rather than from life.

crossRefs.label: Exodus 12 — ye shall put away leaven out of your houses... the LORD's passover
crossRefs.why: "For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us" and the command to "purge out therefore the old leaven" depend entirely on the original feast, where the removal of leaven from every house accompanied the slaying of the lamb and the deliverance from Egypt. The typology explains why the moral demand follows the sacrifice rather than earning it: the houses were swept because the lamb had been killed and the people were leaving.

crossRefs.label: Matthew 18:15-20 — let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican... where two or three are gathered together in my name
crossRefs.why: The procedure and the language both stand behind this chapter. Paul's action is to be taken "when ye are gathered together" and "in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ," with a result that places the offender outside ordinary fellowship, which is the same shape as the graduated correction and the assembly's authority to bind and loose. The parallel is the main text to which appeals about the church's disciplinary competence return.

crossRefs.label: 2 Corinthians 2:6-8 — Sufficient to such a man is this punishment... ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him
crossRefs.why: The later letter shows the discipline working and being lifted, with Paul urging the congregation to restore an offender "lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow" and warning against Satan gaining an advantage. Whether or not the same man is in view, the passage supplies the intended terminus of the sentence in this chapter and rules out reading exclusion as permanent by design.

crossRefs.label: 1 Timothy 1:20 — whom I have delivered unto Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme
crossRefs.why: The only other use of the striking phrase "delivered unto Satan" attaches the same corrective purpose to it, that the offenders "may learn." The parallel weighs against reading the handing over as simple abandonment or a curse, and supports understanding it as removal from the protection of the community into the sphere it has been rescued from, with the intent that the experience teach what argument had not.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes this chapter as an early and concrete exercise of the Church's authority to excommunicate, understood as a genuine juridical act with real spiritual effect rather than an advisory withdrawal of friendship. The elements are all present in the text: a competent authority who "hath judged already," a public verdict, an assembly convened "in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ" and possessing "the power of our Lord Jesus Christ," and a sentence that changes the man's standing before God and the community, "to deliver such an one unto Satan." It is read as medicinal and temporary by nature, ordered to repentance and eventual reconciliation — "that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus" — and so as the seed of the later penitential discipline, in which the Church that excludes is also the Church that absolves and readmits. Paul's confidence that he can judge while "absent in body, but present in spirit" is taken to reflect an apostolic office whose authority is handed on, not a purely personal charism that lapsed with him.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters affirm the reality and necessity of church discipline here — the Reformed tradition in particular counts rightly exercised discipline among the marks of a true church, and takes this chapter as a primary warrant for it. The divergence is over who holds the keys and what the act accomplishes. On this reading Paul does not act over the congregation's head but presses the congregation to act, addressing the whole gathered assembly and rebuking it for failing to do what it already had authority to do; the sentence is declarative, recognizing and announcing a state of affairs the offender's own conduct has created rather than conferring a new one by juridical power. Many also hold that "deliver such an one unto Satan" belongs to Paul's extraordinary apostolic ministry and cannot simply be assumed by later officers, so what continues is exclusion from the fellowship and the table, not a transferable power to consign. Both traditions agree that the act is corporate, public, aimed at repentance, and reversible upon it.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic reading, "with such an one no not to eat" is not limited to declining ordinary hospitality but reaches the Church's central meal, and the chapter's whole movement supports this: the leaven must be purged so that the community may "keep the feast," the reason given is that "Christ our passover is sacrificed for us," and the sacrifice named is the one the Church continues to celebrate. Exclusion from the assembly and exclusion from communion are therefore a single act, which is why the sentence is both so grave and so precisely medicinal — the offender is deprived of the sacramental nourishment of the body he has injured, precisely so that he may hunger for it and return.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings commonly take the immediate reference of "no not to eat" to be shared table fellowship in the broad sense — the common meals and hospitality that in that culture signified acceptance — while readily granting that this includes the Lord's Supper, since in the Corinthian setting the two were largely the same gathering. Where the traditions part is on what the exclusion is from. Fencing the table is widely practiced and defended from this chapter, but the Supper is understood as a means of grace given to faith rather than a sacrificial rite whose withholding operates as a penalty, and the ban is described as the community declining to extend the sign of fellowship to one who has repudiated its substance. Both traditions agree that the offender is to be barred from the church's common meal, and both treat readmission to that meal as the goal.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic interpretation hears "Therefore let us keep the feast" as more than a metaphor for the moral life. The imperative is present and continuous, and it follows immediately upon "Christ our passover is sacrificed for us," so the ongoing feast is the Church's liturgical participation in that one sacrifice — the Passover kept, not merely remembered, with the community's moral condition described as the unleavened bread it brings to a table already set. On this reading the chapter joins ethics and worship at a single point: the leaven is purged because a feast is actually being kept, and the purity in question is the purity required of those who approach an altar.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read "let us keep the feast" as describing the entirety of Christian existence rather than a rite: because the sacrifice was offered once and cannot be repeated, the days of unleavened bread that followed the Passover become an image of the whole life now lived in its light, kept "with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth." The emphasis falls on the finished and unrepeatable character of "Christ our passover is sacrificed for us," and on the fact that Paul's application in context is moral and communal — purge the offender, abandon "malice and wickedness" — rather than liturgical. Both traditions agree that the accomplished sacrifice is the ground of the command and that the feast, however understood, is kept by a community made new rather than by individuals in isolation.
